questions.stem: A 42-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of skin changes on his thighs. He reported that the lesions were occasionally pruritic. He had tried topical and oral antifungals without any response. He was known to have diabetes and was morbidly obese. On examination there were multiple erythematous lesions over both thighs. The lesions were non-tender and cool to touch.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: Corynebacterium minutissimum The description is consistent with a diagnosis of erythrasma, caused by Corynebacterium minutissimum . There is an increased risk of erythrasma in immunocompromised adults (diabetes, elderly, etc.). It may also occur in healthy adults, rarely in children. Corynebacterium minutissimum proliferates in areas of moisture and occlusion (obesity, hyperhidrosis, living in tropical climate, etc.). Coral red fluorescence on Wood’s lamp examination is a classic finding in erythrasma and is due to porphyrin production by C. minutissimum (note test can be false-positive if patients bathed washing away porphyrins prior to exam). In addition to affecting intertriginous areas (groin, axillary, inframammary) C. minutissimum is the number 1 cause of bacterial interdigital infection of the feet. It is clinically indistinguishable from dermatophyte and fungal infections, in this case the only differentiator was the failure of prior topical and oral antifungal therapy. The clinical course and exam findings make CA-MRSA less likely.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q49

questions.question: A cystic fibrosis patient with bronchiectasis has persistent respiratory symptoms despite therapy for Stenotrophomonas and MRSA. After 4 days of therapy, sputum culture grows a chalky-white, non-branching gram-positive bacillus.
questions.question_raw: CF patient with respiratory symptoms despite therapy for Stenotrophomonas and MRSA. Bronchiectasis. Culture on 4 days of therapy grows chalky white colony NON-branching GPB.

parts.text: What is the next test to identify the organism?

parts_raw.text: What is the next test to identify organism?
b) What is the likely diagnosis?

questions.model_answer:
a) Acid-fast (Ziehl-Neelsen or Kinyoun) stain and mycobacterial culture, with MALDI-TOF/species identification, given a chalky-white non-branching GPB emerging on antibacterial therapy suggests a rapidly growing mycobacterium.
b) Nontuberculous mycobacterial infection, most likely Mycobacterium abscessus complex.
questions.beyond_mandell: Mycobacterial identification/management guidance: ATS/IDSA NTM statement (2020).

cohort_answer.text:
Acid fast bacilli smear + culture
Mycobacterium abscessus (tx: Amikacin Imi Clarithro)

questions.question: Sputum from a lung transplant patient grows a gram-positive bacillus that is non-hemolytic, CAMP-positive, motile, and forms pink colonies on subculture.
questions.question_raw: Sputum from a lung transplant patient. GPB, non-hemolytic, CAMP +, motile, swab of colony shows pink colour.
questions.model_answer: a) Rhodococcus equi (salmon-pink mucoid colonies, CAMP-positive, partially acid-fast coccobacillus), a recognized cause of cavitary pneumonia in immunocompromised/transplant hosts.

questions.question: A 5-year-old cystic fibrosis patient recently treated for Stenotrophomonas and MRSA continues to worsen with increasing bronchiectasis and patchy alveolar infiltrates. She is afebrile. Therapy is restarted, and four days in, sputum grows a gram-positive non-branching chalky-white bacillus.
questions.question_raw: PM Q25. 5-year old CF patient with recent course of therapy for Steno + MRSA. Still worsening with increased bronchiectasis + alveolar patchy infiltrates. She is otherwise afebrile. She is again started on therapy, and four days in, sputum is growing a gram positive (non-)branching chalky white bacillus.

parts.text: What is the most likely pathogen?
What is your next step to identify this pathogen?
What are three other Gram-positive rods that can grow aerobically and can cause a similar clinical picture?

parts_raw.text: a) What is the most likely pathogen?
b) What is your next step to identify this pathogen?
What are three other Gram-positive rods that can grow aerobically that can cause a similar clinical picture?

questions.model_answer:
a) Mycobacterium abscessus complex (a rapidly growing NTM; chalky-white non-branching GPB persisting despite antibacterials).
b) Acid-fast smear (Ziehl-Neelsen/Kinyoun) and mycobacterial culture, with species identification by MALDI-TOF or molecular methods.
c) (1) Nocardia species (2) Rhodococcus equi (3) Gordonia or Tsukamurella species.
questions.beyond_mandell: NTM identification/therapy per ATS/IDSA NTM statement (2020).

cohort_answer.text:
Most likely pathogen: Mycobacterium abscessus (Nocardia would have filamentous branching though)
Next step: AFB + culture. Nocardia would be weakly acid fast. Tx: Imipenem, amikacin, septra. Others: mero/linezolid

questions.question: A 51-year-old man on dexamethasone for glioblastoma is admitted with fever and progressively worsening respiratory symptoms over 18 days. CT chest shows multiple non-cavitary nodules measuring 1.5 to 5 cm. He is placed on piperacillin/tazobactam and ciprofloxacin but continues to worsen. After 4 days, respiratory cultures grow dry, yellow colonies, and beaded, filamentous Gram-positive rods are seen on Gram stain.
questions.question_raw: A 51 year-old man, on dexamethasone for a glioblastoma, is admitted with fever and progressively worsening respiratory symptoms x 18 days. CT chest shows multiple non-cavitary nodules measuring 1.5 to 5 cm. Placed on piperacillin/tazobactam and ciprofloxacin, but continues to worsen despite this treatment. After 4 days, respiratory cultures grow dry, yellow colonies. Beaded, filamentous Gram-positive rods are seen on Gram stain.

parts.text: What is the most important next test?
What are three other Gram-positive rods that can grow aerobically that can cause a similar clinical picture?

parts_raw.text: b) What is the most important next test?
c) What are three other Gram-positive rods that can grow aerobically that can cause a similar clinical picture?

questions.model_answer: a) Nocardia species. b) Modified acid-fast stain (modified Kinyoun) — Nocardia is partially acid-fast whereas the main mimic Actinomyces is not; this confirms the presumptive diagnosis. c) (1) Rhodococcus; (2) Gordonia; (3) Tsukamurella (also Streptomyces/Actinomadura).

cohort_answer.text:
a) What is the pathogen? - Nocardia spp
b) What is the most important next test? - Modified Acid fast staining - main DDx = Actinomyces which does not stain with modified acid fast but nocardia does (CT head if you already have identified the pathogen) [source note: Uptodate]
c) What are three other Gram-positive rods that can grow aerobically that can cause a similar clinical picture? - Rhodococcus, Gordonia, Tsukumeullea, Streptomyces - also GPB but not pathogenic so wouldn't include in this answer but FYI
cohort_answer.source: AB 2019 (answer slides (with Gram stain and Acid-Fast Staining images interspersed); speaker notes citing Uptodate for part b)

questions.question: Name four partially acid-fast organisms, then identify the organism shown growing as mucoid/salmon-colored colonies on an agar plate.
questions.question_raw: Q93 2023 Day 2. Name 4 partially acid-fast organisms. Then shown agar plate with mucoid/salmon colored colonies growing and asked to identify. (MICRO)

parts.text: [image-based: identify the organism forming mucoid/salmon colored colonies on the agar plate shown]

parts_raw.text: [image-based: identify the organism forming mucoid/salmon colored colonies on the agar plate shown]

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Nocardia; (2) Rhodococcus; (3) Gordonia; (4) Tsukamurella — all aerobic, branching, partially acid-fast actinomycetes. b) Rhodococcus (Rhodococcus equi) — non-hemolytic, mucoid colonies with characteristic salmon-pink/orange pigment.
questions.beyond_mandell: The mucoid/salmon colony appearance of Rhodococcus is not described in this Nocardia chapter (standard microbiology reference).

cohort_answer.text:
4 partially acid-fast organisms: Nocardia spp; Rhodococcus; Gordonia; Tsukamurella (all partially acid-fast, aerobic, Actinomycetes, branching filamentous bacteria that fragment into rods and cocci).
Mucoid/salmon colonies: Rhodococcus spp - non-hemolytic, round, often mucoid with orange to red/salmon-pink pigment within 4-7 days. (For comparison: Nocardia colonies highly variable, some beta-hemolytic, wrinkly, dry, chalky-white to orange-tan, crumbly; Gordonia colonies smooth, mucoid, adherent, beige/orange/yellow/pink/white to gray; Tsukamurella colonies rhizoid edges, white or creamy to orange.)
